title: Decisions Against Consensus Can't Be Because You're Smarter Than Everyone Else
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines what separates a wise anti-consensus decision from a reckless one. The author distinguishes leaders who buck the group because of a deeply held value or principle from leaders who override consensus simply because they believe they're smarter than the room. Using the infamous 2023 Super Bowl field-turf debacle as a cautionary tale, the piece shows how a leader's refusal to heed expert consensus, driven by personal arrogance rather than principle, led to public failure and his own firing. The takeaway is that going against the group can be legitimate leadership, but only when it is grounded in openly explained values, not ego.
points: Leaders occasionally must go against group consensus, and this can be the right call when grounded in values.
Anti-consensus decisions driven by a leader's belief that they're simply smarter than the team are usually mistakes.
The 2023 Super Bowl turf failure illustrates the cost of ignoring expert consensus out of personal arrogance.
Good leaders explain and debate the value or principle behind an anti-consensus call rather than just overriding others.
Leaders are rarely more knowledgeable than an assembled group of experts.
quotes: Sometimes leaders feel compelled to go against the wisdom of the group. Even when everyone is insisting on north, sometimes leaders believe they must head south.
Leaders who are convicted about an opposing view usually hold a value or principle higher than everyone else.
Leaders who discard the group view because they believe they know better or are smarter than the collective wisdom of the team almost always make a huge mistake.
Instead of heeding the advice or exploring options, the Field Director went against the consensus and selected not to sand the field and watered the turf just days before the game.
He chose not to listen to anyone else because he thought he was smarter and wiser than the collective wisdom of several centuries of experience represented by the team.
In the end, the leader may very well go against the group, but they do so knowing it is principle and not personal vanity that drives the decision.
